name: Guinea Hen
lede: Guinea Hen is a dark olive grey that, in our data, only Maerz and Paul recorded, in 1930, and it is one of the most common colors in our entire painting archive.

sections.title: One dictionary, a very common hue
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's *A Dictionary of Color* places Guinea Hen on plate 16, swatch C4, first recorded in 1918 [1]. No other system in our library repeats the name, though the ISCC-NBS scheme would file a color this close as an olive gray [1]. Its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[dark-olive|Dark Olive]], and the closest common color word is [[umber|Umber]], under ten units away in CIEDE2000 [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within six units of Guinea Hen covers at least five percent of the canvas in 3,038 of our 23,781 paintings, 12.77 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it in 1,993 [2]. That ranks it ahead of 95 percent of the named colors we track, among the most common in the whole archive [2]. It most often plays a mid-tone, in 33 percent of its 1,993 appearances [2].

Peter Hansen is its most devoted painter, in seven of his 18 paintings here, three times the rate of the museums those works come from [2]. It shares canvases with [[moss-grey|Moss Grey]] and [[yellow-grey|Yellow Grey]] more than chance would predict, with lifts of 3.0 and 1.9 [2]. The earliest matching painting dates to 1100, 830 years before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930 — a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof the color existed as a dye that early, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2].
